row.basis: Hebrew raḥûm in the name proclamation
row.note: The Lord declares himself compassionate and gracious, abundant in loyal love; the Hebrew rḥm cognate gives a closely matched divine mercy-name rather than a generic theme.
The next verse couples preservation of love and forgiveness with the refusal to leave guilt unaddressed, closely matching mercy placed beside the coming reckoning.
In a threatened covenant situation God is called El raḥûm and will neither abandon nor forget; this supplies enduring, particular mercy as a divine attribute.
Onkelos renders the merciful-God claim with the Aramaic rḥm family, making an Aramaic divine epithet especially close to the commentary's Rahmân/Rahîm pair.
The communal confession names God as ready to forgive, gracious and compassionate after Israel's refusal; mercy is a praise-name before a plea, not leniency detached from rebellion.
Joel grounds a summons to return in God's gracious and compassionate character and possible relenting from disaster, joining repentance, mercy, and threatened judgment.

row.basis: mercy extended to a hostile city
row.note: Jonah protests the same compassionate-name formula precisely because it spares Nineveh; the scene makes universal mercy morally demanding rather than sentimental.

row.basis: thirteen mercy attributes as penitential practice
row.note: The Talmud turns Exodus 34's self-proclaimed attributes into a pattern for Israel's return after sin, a Jewish reading of mercy-names placed before a request for forgiveness.
In Rabbi Ishmael's sanctuary vision, God's own blessing asks that mercy overcome anger; it directly interprets divine mercy as tempering judgment without abolishing it.

row.basis: justice joined to mercy in creation
row.note: The midrash says God joined mercy to the attribute of justice because the world could not endure justice alone, an explicit interpretive balance for mercy and sovereignty.
Micah joins pardon of iniquity to God's delight in covenantal kindness, giving a compact scriptural account of merciful judgment.

row.basis: Father of mercies in an opening blessing
row.note: Paul's doxology identifies God as the Father of mercies before describing consolation, a Christian praise-form in which mercy is a defining divine name.
The Peshitta uses its rḥm family for God's tender mercy when that mercy sends the dawn; the Syriac cognate carries both the divine attribute and its active visitation.

row.basis: tender mercy that visits and guides
row.note: The Benedictus makes God's tender mercy the cause of a dawn from on high, whose effect is to guide feet into peace; mercy precedes and enables guidance.
Before any human response, God is described as rich in mercy and great love, matching the commentary's stress on mercy named before an appeal is made.
The following verse makes the prior mercy concrete by giving life while people are dead in transgressions, an enacted rather than merely felt compassion.
The verse explicitly reverses initiative: God loved and sent before people loved him, closely paralleling provision given before a child can ask or know.

row.basis: father runs before the son's completed plea
row.note: The father sees the returning son while he is still far away, runs, embraces, and kisses him before the confession is finished; mercy anticipates the request.

row.basis: throne, mercy, and help in need
row.note: Believers approach a throne to receive mercy and find grace for timely help, a close meeting of royal authority, mercy, and the later cry for aid.
Daniel asks God to hear and act not on Israel's righteousness but on God's great mercies, making petition rest on a mercy already confessed.
The verse sets the Hebrew verb for compassion beside reḥem, womb, in one maternal question; it is the clearest Hebrew meeting of the root's mercy and womb senses.
A mother's nursing care may fail, but God's refusal to forget Zion does not; the comparison makes maternal nurture an image of reliable divine mercy.
God addresses Israel as a people borne from the belly and carried from the womb, closely matching the commentary's protected child before conscious asking.
Even to old age God will carry, bear, and save; this extends womb-like care into enduring, settled mercy rather than a single rescue.

row.basis: teaching an unknowing child to walk
row.note: God says he taught Ephraim to walk and took the child in his arms, though Ephraim did not know who healed him; care and growth precede recognition.
The wilderness memory compares God's care to a man carrying his son all the way, supplying a paternal counterpart to the commentary's sustaining womb-home.

row.basis: parental yearning and raḥam for Ephraim
row.note: The Lord calls Ephraim a dear child and says he will surely have compassion; the Hebrew rḥm language joins parental inward concern to restoration after judgment.
God finds Jerusalem as a helpless newborn in blood and commands it to live, a stark image of life-giving intervention before the recipient can request anything.

row.basis: life, loyal love, and preserving care
row.note: Job credits God with life, steadfast love, and watchful preservation, a direct analogue for mercy as sustained nurture rather than bare emotion.
Joseph's compassion is stirred at the sight of Benjamin; this human use of the Hebrew rḥm family supplies the commentary's distinction between a divine title and human merciful action.
Jacob asks El Shaddai to grant raḥamim before the Egyptian ruler so his sons may return; mercy is directed to a vulnerable family in a concrete crisis.
The martyr's mother says she did not herself give life, breath, or arrange her children's elements in the womb, placing maternal bearing under the Creator's work.
The Creator who formed humanity is said to give life and breath back in mercy, joining womb-formation, divine compassion, and resurrection.
God's great mercy causes believers to be born anew into living hope through resurrection, a Christian pairing of mercy with generated life and future hope.
The text denies that salvation follows prior righteous works and locates it in mercy through washing of rebirth, an explicit before-request gift.
In the wilderness, God's abundant mercies keep the cloud from departing and continue to lead the people; mercy becomes direction on a path.
Paul appeals by God's mercies for embodied worship, a close formal counterpart to mercy being named before the human voice turns to worship and service.
God executes justice for orphan and widow and loves the resident alien by giving food and clothing, exactly joining compassion to material provision for the weak.

row.basis: imitation of God's care for the stranger
row.note: The command to love the resident alien follows God's own food-and-clothing care, making human mercy an imitation of divine action.

row.basis: mercy and compassion toward one's brother
row.note: The prophetic command joins just judgment to showing kindness and compassion to one another, matching the commentary's soft heart becoming social practice.
The next command specifies those who must not be oppressed, giving concrete faces to mercy's preferential attention to the weak.

row.basis: feed, shelter, clothe, and own flesh
row.note: True devotion shares bread with the hungry, houses the homeless, clothes the naked, and does not hide from one's own kin; mercy reaches both need and kinship.
Sirach requires enduring care for a father in old age, a direct reciprocal response to the parental nurture developed in the womb and upbringing imagery.
Children and grandchildren are told to care first for their household and make return to their parents, giving a New Testament form to gratitude for received care.
The Talmud reads walking after God as clothing the naked, visiting the sick, comforting mourners, and burying the dead; mercy is defined as costly action.
The saying that one compassionate to creatures receives compassion from Heaven makes the reciprocity between divine and human mercy explicit.
Sirach tells the reader to become a father to orphans and a husband to their mother, turning family imagery into care for the exposed and weak.

row.basis: God's mercy over every living thing
row.note: Sirach contrasts human compassion for a neighbor with the Lord's mercy for every living creature, a remarkably exact universal-versus-particular mercy pairing.

row.basis: bread for hungry and clothing for naked
row.note: Tobit's instruction makes almsgiving bodily and concrete, closely matching mercy that reaches a needy person rather than remaining an inner feeling.

row.basis: compassion that crosses toward a wounded stranger
row.note: The Samaritan is moved with compassion on seeing the injured man, beginning the movement from inward response to costly help.
Jesus identifies the true neighbor as the one who did mercy, explicitly making mercy an act rather than a sentiment.
James rejects a peaceful blessing for the hungry and cold when it provides none of the body's needs, directly testing compassion by its result.
The writer asks how divine love remains in a person who sees a sibling's need, closes the inner compassion, and withholds goods; emotion must become provision.
Religion acceptable to God includes visiting orphans and widows in their distress, a concentrated New Testament version of mercy toward the vulnerable.
Jesus commands disciples to be merciful as their Father is merciful, making divine mercy the source and norm of human conduct.

row.basis: received mercy obligates mercy to another
row.note: The king's mercy toward a debtor becomes the reason the servant should have shown mercy to a fellow servant, linking grace received to mercy enacted.
Jesus cites God's desire for mercy over sacrifice in response to table fellowship with sinners, prioritizing merciful practice over a merely cultic appearance.
Christ is called a merciful and faithful high priest who aids his siblings; this is a precise Christian instance of mercy predicated of a human agent.

row.basis: mercy to all and patience for repentance
row.note: God is merciful to all, overlooks sins, and aims at repentance; wide mercy is joined to moral return rather than indifference to evil.
God spares all because all are his and is named lover of the living, closely tying universal mercy to creatorly ownership.

row.basis: pity for a city and its animals
row.note: God's pity extends to morally confused Nineveh and its many cattle, a concrete scriptural scene of mercy broader than a chosen human group.
At creation's interrogation, God asks who provides prey for ravens when they cry; it supplies the commentary's bird-and-providence image in its own setting.
Jesus directs attention to birds whom the heavenly Father feeds, making creaturely sustenance a sign of divine care before human anxiety or request.
Paul calls seasonal rains and fruitful harvests God's ongoing beneficence to peoples who did not yet know him, closely matching rain as visible mercy.
The Father's rain falls on both righteous and unrighteous, a specific image of indiscriminate provision that tests the commentary's expansive mercy.

row.basis: life, breath, and all things for all
row.note: Paul's creator neither needs human service nor lacks anything, since he gives all people life, breath, and everything; universal dependence is the point.

row.basis: mercy on all after universal disobedience
row.note: Paul holds universal confinement in disobedience together with the purpose of mercy on all, a deliberately broad mercy-and-judgment formulation.
Paul's citation, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy,” supplies a distinct Christian argument about mercy's particular bestowal alongside its wider language elsewhere.
Israel must bless God after eating and being satisfied in the good land, a concrete response of gratitude to completed provision.
Jeshurun grows fat and forsakes the God who made him, a counter-scene to the commentary's call to turn received blessing into gratitude.
The healed Samaritan falls at Jesus' feet, glorifies God, and gives thanks; bodily benefit becomes the grateful response the commentary seeks.
Jesus' question about the absent nine exposes the contrary pattern: mercy received without praise or thanks.
Those who knew God neither glorified him nor gave thanks, despite the created order, paralleling the commentary's warning that benefit can be met with forgetfulness.
Lamentations asserts that the Lord's loyal love and compassions do not end, a direct image of mercy that remains rather than flashes once.
The daily renewal of God's compassions makes continuing mercy temporal and repeated, resonating with the commentary's settled Rahîm dimension.
The poem says that though God causes grief, he will have compassion according to abundant love; hard experience is not its final meaning.

row.basis: humanly evil act turned to preserving good
row.note: Joseph distinguishes his brothers' evil intent from God's intention to preserve many lives, giving a biblical model for a severe appearance whose end is protective good.

row.basis: the Lord compassionate and merciful after Job
row.note: James invokes Job's endurance and the Lord's eventual purpose to call the Lord compassionate and merciful, explicitly reading suffering through a merciful outcome.
The Lord disciplines those he loves; the verse supplies a closely related claim that a painful divine act can be care rather than abandonment.
The prophet directly asks God to remember mercy in wrath, an unusually concise counterpart to mercy and judgment held together.
James warns of judgment without mercy for the merciless and then says mercy triumphs over judgment, keeping ethical seriousness inside mercy-talk.
God's kindness, forbearance, and patience are meant to lead to repentance, so delayed judgment is an active moral mercy.
The Lord's apparent delay is explained as patience aimed at repentance rather than destruction, closely pairing future judgment with merciful restraint.

row.basis: rebuke and discipline of the beloved
row.note: The speaker rebukes and disciplines those he loves and calls for zeal and repentance, a compact mercy-and-warning sequence.

row.basis: mercy that does not depart after anger
row.note: After an image of abandonment, God promises that covenantal love will not depart and identifies himself as the one having compassion on Zion.

row.basis: God found by those who did not ask
row.note: The Lord says he was ready to be sought by people who did not ask and found by those who did not seek, directly echoing mercy before a request.

row.basis: promised mercy and remembered sin no more
row.note: The new-covenant promise makes divine mercy the ground for not remembering sins, a stable pledged mercy rather than a momentary feeling.

row.basis: mercy asked by the penitent sinner
row.note: The tax collector's short appeal for mercy comes within a judgment parable and frames the sinner's hope in God's mercy rather than self-assertion.
The Benedictus calls God's saving action the performance of mercy promised to the ancestors and remembrance of covenant, linking mercy to lasting commitment.

row.basis: God as father and Davidic king as son
row.note: In its royal covenant setting, God promises paternal and filial language for David's heir; it is a biblical sonship pattern relevant to the commentary's rejection of divine child attribution.
Luke calls the miraculously conceived child holy and Son of God, a direct Christian counter-claim to the commentary's insistence that Rahmân has no child.

row.basis: known and set apart before birth
row.note: God's knowing and setting apart Jeremiah before formation in the womb gives a prophetic, rather than maternal, counterpart to divine attention within the womb.

row.basis: set apart from the mother's womb
row.note: Paul describes his calling as God's grace setting him apart from his mother's womb; the link is a vocation-specific form of prenatal divine purpose.
Daniel begins prayer by naming the great covenant-keeping God before asking anything, a formal prayer sequence comparable to mercy's placement before later requests.

row.basis: hallowing the Father's name before needs
row.note: The Lord's Prayer begins with the Father's name and kingdom before bread, forgiveness, and rescue are requested; it offers a related liturgical ordering.

row.basis: gracious divine face in a priestly blessing
row.note: The priestly blessing invokes God's shining face and grace over recipients before any individual petition; it is a nearby ritual form rather than the same mercy vocabulary.

row.basis: a divine name for calling and remembrance
row.note: God gives Moses a name to be invoked and remembered through generations, a distinct biblical setting for a name that is more than an abstract description.
Paul begins from an altar to an unknown god and promises to declare the one worshiped without knowledge, resembling the commentary's question about an unfamiliar divine name.

row.basis: the unknown one identified as Creator
row.note: The next claim identifies that unknown God as maker of world and heaven; together with the prior verse it supplies a formal analogue to a questioned name answered by creation.
Micah joins justice, love of covenant kindness, and humble walking with God; it gives an Israelite ethical counterpart to the gentle walk of Rahmân's servants.

row.basis: meekness and inheritance of the earth
row.note: The beatitude links meekness with inheriting the earth, a specific Christian image adjacent to the commentary's servants who walk gently on earth.
Paul contrasts a spirit of slavery producing fear with adoption as children who cry to God as Father; it offers a Christian reconfiguration of the servant relationship.
The son does not bear the father's guilt and the father does not bear the son's; this juridical rule gives a concrete limit to kinship when judgment is in view.

row.basis: silence before the day of the Lord
row.note: Zephaniah commands silence before the Lord because his day is near, a close Hebrew prophetic analogue to hushed voices before the merciful sovereign's day.
Paul describes every mouth stopped and the whole world accountable to God, a juridical silence that illuminates the commentary's day-of-reckoning scene.
Heaven falls silent before the trumpet judgments, an apocalyptic visual and auditory parallel to the commentary's restrained voices before divine dominion.

row.basis: all earth silent before the enthroned Lord
row.note: The earth is ordered to silence before the Lord in his holy temple; this is a non-identical but precise throne-and-silence meeting.

row.basis: all creatures passing before divine judgment
row.note: The Mishnah imagines all who enter the world passing before God on Rosh Hashanah, giving a Jewish liturgical horizon to universal appearance before the owner of the day.
Augustine argues that the omnipotent God permits evil only while able to draw good from it; this is a Christian interpretive bridge for mercy whose first appearance can be severe.
God compares his consolation of Jerusalem to a mother comforting her child; it extends the commentary's maternal imagery beyond gestation into restorative presence.
The Benedictus moves from covenant mercy to deliverance so that people may serve God without fear, a nearby Christian sequence from mercy to worship.
Daniel's sleepers awake to everlasting life or contempt, a Jewish resurrection-and-reckoning scene that supplies the day backdrop for mercy's promise of rising.

row.basis: mercy and compassion by divine declaration
row.note: God proclaims that he will be gracious and compassionate as he chooses; the Hebrew rḥm forms give a direct antecedent for mercy both expansive and particularly bestowed.

row.basis: poor person's cloak and divine compassion
row.note: The law requires returning a poor person's sole covering before night because God hears the cry and is compassionate, joining divine character to practical aid.
David chooses to fall into the Lord's hand during punishment because the Lord's compassions are many, a specific mercy-and-reckoning scene.
Solomon asks God to forgive Israel and grant it compassion before its captors; divine forgiveness is meant to generate merciful treatment in a human relationship.
The Lord is gracious and compassionate to Israel because of covenant and does not yet destroy or cast it away, an enduring mercy within historical judgment.
After the difficult command against an apostate city, God promises mercy, compassion, and multiplication; it is a close case of a hard act framed by later good.
God's compassion is enacted as return and gathering from exile, making mercy a concrete restoration of a scattered family.

row.basis: pity moved by the oppressed's groaning
row.note: The Lord raises saviors and is moved to pity by Israel's groaning under oppressors, a narrative of compassion becoming deliverance.
Israel cries in distress and God gives saviors according to great mercies, pairing a plea for help with prior merciful intervention.
The confession says God's many mercies prevented him from making an end of Israel or forsaking it, directly expressing lasting mercy after rebellion.

row.basis: return to a gracious and compassionate God
row.note: The call to return says God is gracious and compassionate and will not turn his face away, closely joining return, divine face, and mercy.

row.basis: the just Lord waiting to show compassion
row.note: Isaiah names the Lord as a God of justice who waits to be gracious and rises to show compassion, an explicit mercy-and-judgment balance.

row.basis: made from the womb and helped
row.note: The Lord identifies himself as maker and former from the womb, then promises help; this tightly joins prenatal formation with protective care.

row.basis: former from the womb and sole Creator
row.note: The Redeemer who formed Israel from the womb is also the one who alone made all things, directly meeting womb imagery with cosmic creative sovereignty.
After saying Zion was forsaken briefly, God promises to gather her with great compassion, a necessary earlier movement in the mercy sequence continued at 54:10.
The returning wicked person finds God's compassion and abundant pardon, a direct mercy-and-repentance formulation.
God summons faithless Israel to return and says he will not keep anger forever because he is merciful, giving mercy a concrete role in judgment.
God promises never to turn from doing his people good and to preserve their reverence, an unusually explicit account of continuing beneficent care.

row.basis: rejoicing to do good and plant securely
row.note: God's delight in doing his people good and planting them securely turns covenant mercy into settled restoration.

row.basis: no pleasure in a wicked person's death
row.note: God calls the wicked to turn and live rather than die, grounding warning and judgment in a life-seeking divine intention.
Daniel confesses that mercies and forgiveness belong to the Lord even though the people have rebelled, a prayerful mercy-before-pardon formulation.
The person who confesses and leaves sin receives mercy, giving a wisdom-text counterpart to mercy that enables repentance without excusing wrongdoing.
Lamentations says God does not willingly afflict or grieve human beings, sharpening the preceding claim that grief can coexist with compassion.

row.basis: father sparing a serving son on the day
row.note: God promises to spare those who serve him as a man spares a son; mercy, filial imagery, service, and the coming day meet in one verse.
God's return to Jerusalem with mercy entails rebuilding his house there, showing mercy as restoration rather than an inward disposition.
God saves and brings back divided houses because he has compassion, treating them as though he had not rejected them.
God hears enslaved people's groaning and remembers covenant, a concrete sequence of suffering, divine attention, and remembered relation.
God describes seeing, hearing, and knowing Israel's suffering, supplying the emotional and attentive side of merciful rescue.

row.basis: coming down to deliver and lead
row.note: God's response to the preceding cry is descent, liberation, and leading to a land, a full action-pattern for mercy.

row.basis: one maker forming both in the womb
row.note: Job grounds just treatment of servants in the single God who formed master and servant in the womb, joining womb origin to social mercy.
God keeps covenant and loyal love with those who love him through a thousand generations, a durable and relational form of mercy.

row.basis: not hardening heart against poor kin
row.note: The law forbids hardening the heart or closing the hand against a poor brother or sister, explicitly pairing inner hardness with failure of kin-directed mercy.

row.basis: opening the hand and supplying need
row.note: The required alternative is to open the hand freely and lend enough for the need, making mercy an adequate material response.
Generosity must be given without inner resentment, a close ethical counterpart to the commentary's distinction between a gift and a reproached gift.
The Israelite must support a brother who becomes poor so that he can live nearby, a direct scriptural meeting of kinship and sustaining care.

row.basis: giving to poor as lending to the Lord
row.note: Kindness to the poor is treated as a loan to the Lord, connecting help for a weak person to God's own accounting and return.

row.basis: closing the ear to a poor cry
row.note: The person who ignores the poor person's cry will himself cry without answer, a sharp reciprocal warning about refusing mercy.
The opening prophetic call specifies defending the orphan and pleading for the widow, giving concrete content to a softened and just heart.

row.basis: pouring oneself out for hungry and afflicted
row.note: The fast Isaiah commends expends oneself for the hungry and satisfies the afflicted; light then rises out of darkness, connecting mercy to costly action and renewal.
Daniel tells the king to break with sin by righteousness and with iniquity by showing mercy to the oppressed, making mercy a corrective political act.

row.basis: bread for hungry and clothing for naked
row.note: The righteous person gives bread to the hungry and covers the naked, a close prophetic counterpart to mercy measured by what reaches the weak.
Wisdom says God's manner of judging teaches the righteous to be kind and gives hope of repentance, directly linking mercy, justice, and ethical imitation.
Sirach calls the Lord compassionate and merciful, forgiving sins and saving in affliction, a compact wisdom formula for mercy under distress.

row.basis: mercy and forgiveness for those who return
row.note: The text praises the Lord's great mercy and forgiveness toward those who turn to him, extending the return-and-mercy pattern into later Jewish wisdom.

row.basis: afflicting, showing mercy, and raising from death
row.note: Tobit's hymn says God both afflicts and shows mercy, leads down to Hades and brings up again; this strongly parallels mercy, hardship, and resurrection in one confession.

row.basis: great mercy shown in a birth and shared by kin
row.note: Elizabeth's neighbors and relatives hear that the Lord magnified mercy to her and rejoice, joining pregnancy, kinship, and communal recognition of mercy.
The dawn from on high guides feet into the way of peace, the necessary continuation of Luke 1:78's tender-mercy claim and a direct mercy-to-guidance sequence.

row.basis: kindness to ungrateful and evil people
row.note: Jesus grounds enemy-love in the Most High's kindness to the ungrateful and wicked, a particularly demanding account of broad divine mercy.

row.basis: bandaging and paying for the wounded man
row.note: The Samaritan's compassion becomes wounds treated, transport, lodging, and payment, supplying the concrete middle action between feeling compassion and being named merciful.

row.basis: dead and alive, lost and found
row.note: The father's celebration interprets the restored son as dead now alive and lost now found, a mercy scene with resurrection-shaped language.
The tax collector, rather than the self-assured worshiper, goes home justified; this is the necessary outcome of the preceding appeal for mercy in a judgment setting.
The Son of Man's stated mission is to seek and save the lost, a concentrated Christian expression of merciful initiative before the lost can restore themselves.
Jesus is moved with compassion, touches a leper, and heals him; compassion crosses impurity boundaries and becomes bodily restoration.
Jesus sends the healed man home to tell what the Lord has done and how he had mercy on him, linking received aid to grateful witness among kin.
Jesus sees a crowd as sheep without a shepherd, has compassion, and begins to teach them; mercy here supplies instruction as well as care.

row.basis: compassion that will not send the hungry away
row.note: Jesus names his compassion for a crowd without food and refuses to dismiss them hungry, closely matching mercy as feeding the weak.
The Lord sees a widow grieving her only son, has compassion, and addresses her sorrow; the maternal and vulnerable situation makes the link specific.
Jesus compares his desired protection of Jerusalem's children to a bird gathering its brood, a maternal shelter image beside the commentary's protecting womb-home.
The king is moved with compassion, releases the servant, and forgives the debt, supplying the prior mercy that grounds the later command to forgive another.
The parable closes with judgment on those who do not forgive from the heart, keeping received mercy morally serious and accountable.

row.basis: service to the least received by the King
row.note: The king identifies care for hungry, stranger, naked, sick, and imprisoned people as care received by himself, binding mercy to the final royal judgment.

row.basis: refusing the least as refusal before judgment
row.note: The negative verdict treats withholding care from the least as withholding it from the judge, a counter-scene to mercy enacted toward the weak.

row.basis: poor sibling lacking clothes and food
row.note: The verse supplies the concrete needy sibling whose unmet need makes the following empty blessing morally insufficient.
Christ dies for the weak at the right time, a specific Christian claim that saving action meets incapacity rather than prior achievement.

row.basis: love acting while people are sinners
row.note: God demonstrates love in Christ's death while people are still sinners, another explicit formulation of mercy taking the first step.
God's consolation in affliction equips believers to comfort others, extending the Father-of-mercies title into reciprocal human care.
Believers are commanded to be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving as God forgave them; inward tenderness and concrete reconciliation are held together.
The community is to put on compassion with kindness and humility, a direct ethical counterpart to merciful servants walking gently.

row.basis: nursing mother caring for her children
row.note: Paul compares his gentle care for the community to a nursing mother caring for her own children, a close Christian maternal-nurture image.

row.basis: divine kindness and love for humanity appearing
row.note: The appearance of God's kindness and philanthropy is the necessary opening of the mercy-and-rebirth claim in the following verse.
The divine parent disciplines for the believers' good so they may share holiness, clarifying the beneficial end of the hard action named at 12:6.

row.basis: from not receiving mercy to receiving it
row.note: The community's identity is defined by having once lacked mercy and now received it, a direct transformation by bestowed mercy.
The God of all grace restores, confirms, strengthens, and establishes people after they suffer a little while, a sustained-care reading of hardship.
The command to love in deed and truth completes the preceding warning about withholding goods, making action the proof of compassion.
The community is told to have mercy on those who doubt, a direct interpersonal use of mercy toward spiritual weakness.

row.basis: saving from fire with fearful mercy
row.note: Mercy is joined to rescuing some from fire and maintaining fear of corruption, closely holding compassion and grave danger together.

row.basis: shepherding, living water, and wiped tears
row.note: The Lamb shepherds the redeemed, leads them to springs of living water, and God wipes their tears; final sovereignty is rendered as tender provision.
Jesus promises not to leave disciples as orphans but to come to them, a specific parental-care image for mercy that prevents abandonment.

row.basis: the Word as unique Son from the Father
row.note: John claims that the Word became flesh and bears the glory of the unique Son from the Father, a fuller Christian counter-narrative to the commentary's denial of divine child language.

row.basis: mercy and forgiveness as reciprocal discipline
row.note: The early Christian letter exhorts mercy and forgiveness in the measure one hopes to receive them, extending Gospel mercy into a communal rule.

row.basis: Hagar naming the God who sees her
row.note: The pregnant and afflicted Hagar calls God the one who sees her; the connection is a maternal vulnerability answered by divine attention rather than the rḥm vocabulary itself.

row.basis: water opened to mother and child
row.note: God opens Hagar's eyes to a well for her endangered child, a narrative of preemptive provision in a maternal crisis.
The shepherd gives eternal life and says no one will snatch the sheep from his hand, a pastoral image of enduring protective care.

row.basis: the teacher who instructs and reminds
row.note: The Spirit is sent to teach and remind disciples, a Christian teaching-and-guidance scene adjacent to the commentary's Rahmân who teaches.

row.basis: prayers and alms remembered before God
row.note: Cornelius's prayers and alms rise as a memorial before God, linking practical generosity and prayer without making either a purchase of mercy.

row.basis: doing good to all and to the household of faith
row.note: The command combines broad beneficence with a particular household obligation, a modest Christian analogue to wide and kin-directed care.

row.basis: gifts used to serve one another
row.note: Each received gift is to be used in service to others as stewardship of varied grace, a downstream ethic of gifts becoming help.

row.basis: waiting for mercy into eternal life
row.note: Believers keep themselves in God's love while awaiting mercy leading to eternal life, a future-facing mercy frame for the day of fulfillment.

row.basis: acts of lovingkindness without fixed measure
row.note: The Mishnah counts deeds of lovingkindness among practices whose fruit is enjoyed now and whose principal remains for the future, giving mercy an ongoing communal form.
The Didache orders unhesitating giving to those who ask and grounds distribution in the Father's gifts, a later Christian rule for mercy before return.

row.basis: mercy passing at the judgment seat
row.note: In the commonly cited English numbering, 4 Ezra says compassion passes away when the Most High appears for judgment; it is a Jewish apocalyptic counterweight to mercy framing the final day.
